speaker: Maya
text: Last time: the collision, Europe crashing into the Americas, and Spain grabbing an empire. This time: what Spain built with it, and why England spent decades trying to steal it. Three boxes on your sheet: Potosí, the Black Legend, and England's challenge. Circle the ones you couldn't explain right now. Eight minutes, and you'll check all three off.

speaker: Marcus
text: Start with the money, because everything else follows it. In 1545, silver is found at Potosí, a mountain in what's now Bolivia. A year later, another huge strike at Zacatecas, in Mexico. Potosí grew into one of the biggest cities on earth, up there with London and Paris, and for the rest of the 1500s, most of the world's silver came out of Spanish America.

speaker: Maya
text: Wait, pieces of eight? Like pirate treasure?

speaker: Marcus
text: Those exact coins. Spanish silver dollars, minted from this metal. And the crown took a cut of everything: the royal fifth, twenty percent off the top. The rest flooded the world economy. Silver dug out of a Bolivian mountain ended up paying for silk and spices from Asia.

speaker: Maya
text: So the whole economy runs on shiny rocks?

speaker: Marcus
text: The idea even has a name: mercantilism. A nation's wealth is the gold and silver it stockpiles. And all that silver pouring in pushed prices up across Europe for a century. Historians call it the price revolution.

speaker: Maya
text: Okay, that's disgustingly rich. Who's digging it out?

speaker: Marcus
text: Mostly forced Native labor, at least at first. At Potosí it was called the mita. The Spanish took the Inca labor draft and reorganized it in the 1570s: villages sent a rotating share of men, about one year in seven. Down in the mines they crushed ore and mixed it with mercury to pull the silver out, a trick the Spanish also brought in the 1570s, breathing the fumes the whole time. It killed huge numbers of workers. Later, paid hands joined them, but the draft never went away.

speaker: Maya
text: One year in seven.

speaker: Marcus
text: In the dark, breathing mercury.

speaker: Maya
text: And the crown's just... fine with that?

speaker: Marcus
text: The crown needed the money. That was the whole debate. And silver wasn't the only machine. The Franciscans built missions across the frontier. They said conversion, and they meant it. But the missions also controlled Native labor and anchored Spanish towns wherever they went. Then there's the social ladder. Peninsulares, literally 'from the peninsula,' Spaniards born in Spain, at the top. Criollos, Spaniards born in the Americas, a step down. Below them: mestizos of mixed Spanish and Native ancestry, Indigenous peoples, enslaved Africans, and the mixed castas. Part custom, part law. It decided who could hold office and who paid tribute.

speaker: Marcus
text: That machine ran the empire. England told a different story about it. Starting in the 1500s, English and Dutch writers painted Spain as uniquely cruel. A Flemish engraver named Theodor de Bry made lurid prints to prove it: Spaniards setting dogs on Native villagers while priests looked on. Centuries later, the whole package got a name: the Black Legend.

speaker: Maya
text: Dogs? On villagers? Okay, that's horrifying.

speaker: Marcus
text: That was the point. Nothing sold pamphlets like horror.

speaker: Maya
text: So was any of it true?

speaker: Marcus
text: Some of it, yes. Real accounts made the best propaganda. A Spanish friar, Las Casas, had written real accounts of the cruelty decades earlier. His reports even sparked a formal debate at Valladolid in 1550 over whether conquering and enslaving Native peoples could ever be just. The English and Dutch took those accounts and cranked up the horror, while leaving out the part where they were doing plenty of brutal things themselves.

speaker: Maya
text: But if the cruelty was real, where's the lie?

speaker: Marcus
text: The lie was the word 'uniquely.' Spain was brutal, and so was everyone else building an empire. The Legend just never mentioned them. And it worked. It gave England a moral excuse to go after Spanish ships.

speaker: Marcus
text: The empire's built. England couldn't beat Spain at colonies, so it beat Spain at sea, starting with Francis Drake.

speaker: Maya
text: Pirate phase! I had one in fourth grade. Eye patch and everything.

speaker: Marcus
text: Then you'll love this. Drake was a privateer, a pirate with a license from the queen. From 1577 to 1580 he sailed around the entire world, the first Englishman to do it and only the second expedition ever, after Magellan's, robbing Spanish ports and ships the whole way. Off South America he caught a treasure ship so loaded the Spanish crew had nicknamed it Cacafuego, roughly "fire-pooper," and yes, that's the polite translation.

speaker: Maya
text: I'm sorry, what?

speaker: Marcus
text: Sailors. The queen's share alone roughly matched an entire year of crown revenue. Elizabeth knighted him aboard his own ship. The Spanish called him El Draque, the Dragon.

speaker: Maya
text: Okay, Dragon is a great nickname. But stealing ships isn't a colony.

speaker: Marcus
text: Right. So Raleigh tries the real thing. 1587: a group of about 117 English colonists lands on Roanoke Island, off what's now North Carolina — including Virginia Dare, the first English kid born in the Americas. Their governor, John White, sails back to England for supplies.

speaker: Maya
text: And this is the Pocahontas one?

speaker: Marcus
text: Jamestown, twenty years later. Different colony. White gets stuck in England. War with Spain, no ships to spare. When he finally gets back in 1590, everyone's gone. One clue: the word CROATOAN carved into a palisade post.

speaker: Maya
text: That's genuinely creepy. So... the Spanish got them?

speaker: Marcus
text: No bodies. No signs of a battle, either, and no distress signal. The leading theory now: they didn't vanish, they joined the local Croatoan people. But nobody's fully sure.

speaker: Maya
text: Croatoan. That's Hatteras Island now, right?

speaker: Marcus
text: Same island, new name. America's first unsolved mystery.

speaker: Maya
text: So England's big colonial debut is a ghost town. Then what?

speaker: Marcus
text: Then 1588. Philip's motives stacked up: Drake's raid on Cádiz the year before, Elizabeth's money behind the Dutch rebels, and the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots, the Catholic heir. So he sends about 130 ships to invade England and put a Catholic back on the throne. Literally back, by the way. Philip had been married to Elizabeth's Catholic half-sister, Mary I.

speaker: Maya
text: Her brother-in-law invades? Families are complicated.

speaker: Marcus
text: The English meet them in the Channel in smaller, quicker ships, and at night they send burning ships drifting into the Spanish anchorage at Calais. Panic. Then storms smash the survivors trying to sail home around Scotland. Roughly half the fleet never comes back.

speaker: Maya
text: So for the test — 1588, why does it matter?

speaker: Marcus
text: Protestant England survives, which keeps the door open for everything England does next. And the myth cracks: Spain can be beaten. Spain rebuilt. The empire had decades left in it. But after 1588, England stops thinking like a pirate and starts thinking like a planter.

speaker: Maya
text: Three boxes, let's land them. One: Potosí. Silver mountain, 1545. And the crown took... twenty percent?

speaker: Marcus
text: Twenty percent, the royal fifth. 1545, a mountain of silver in Bolivia. Forced Native labor under the mita, mercury to pull the metal out. The money that ran the empire.

speaker: Maya
text: Two: the Black Legend. England and the Dutch exaggerated Spanish cruelty:

speaker: Marcus
text: Exaggerated, not invented, and it gave England its excuse.

speaker: Maya
text: Three: England's challenge.

speaker: Marcus
text: Drake's privateers, the Roanoke disappearance, then 1588. Philip sends about 130 ships to invade England. Between the fireships, the English guns, and the storms off Scotland, roughly half never make it home. Spain survives, but the fear of Spain doesn't.

speaker: Maya
text: Two questions, AP-shaped. Say your answer before I give it. One: a 1598 engraving shows Spaniards setting dogs on Native villagers. It was printed in Frankfurt by a man who never crossed the Atlantic. What's the point of a source like that?

speaker: Maya
text: Propaganda. Black Legend material. Real cruelty underneath, exaggerated to turn readers against Spain and excuse England's own ambitions.

speaker: Maya
text: Two: why ship mercury across an ocean to Potosí?

speaker: Maya
text: For the silver. Mercury pulled it out of the ore, and the crown's cut, twenty percent, the royal fifth, funded the empire.

speaker: Maya
text: Check your three boxes. Episode three in the books. Next time: England stops raiding and starts planting — Jamestown, 1607.

speaker: Marcus
text: Spain built an empire on silver.

speaker: Maya
text: And England spent decades trying to take it apart.
